statute_title: Operating a Motor Vehicle While Under the Influence of Alcohol or Drugs
offense_class: Unclassified Misdemeanor (first DWAI); Misdemeanor (first DWI); Class E Felony (second within 10 years); Class D Felony (third within 10 years)
penalty_max: 15 days (DWAI); 1 year (first DWI); 4 years (second — Class E Felony); 7 years (third — Class D Felony)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
Upon a public highway or in a parking lot
While in an intoxicated condition or while ability was impaired by alcohol or drugs
BAC of .08 or more (per se DWI) or .05–.07 (DWAI)
enhancements: Child under 15 in vehicle (Leandra's Law — Class E Felony under § 1192(2-a)(b))
Second offense within 10 years (Class E Felony)
Third offense within 10 years (Class D Felony)
notes: New York distinguishes DWAI (impaired, .05–.07), DWI (.08+), and Aggravated DWI (.18+). Leandra's Law makes DWI with a child under 15 in the vehicle a Class E Felony even on first offense. Conditional discharge, probation, or ignition interlock commonly imposed.

offense_class: Unclassified Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
While intoxicated (common law DWI) or with BAC .08 or higher (per se DWI)
No prior DWI conviction within 10 years
mandatory_minimum: 6-month license revocation; ignition interlock device; mandatory fine $500–$1,000
enhancements: BAC .18 or higher (Aggravated DWI — higher fine and longer revocation)
Child under 15 (Leandra's Law — Class E Felony)
notes: Mandatory $500–$1,000 fine. 6-month license revocation. Drinking Driver Program (DDP) required. Ignition interlock device required for at least 12 months. Conditional discharge common for first offenders.

offense_class: Class E Felony (second within 10 years); Class D Felony (third within 10 years)
penalty_min: 5 days or 30 days community service (second); 10 days or 60 days community service (third)
penalty_max: 4 years (second — Class E Felony); 7 years (third — Class D Felony)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle while intoxicated
BAC .08 or higher, or impaired driving ability
One or more prior DWI convictions within 10 years
mandatory_minimum: 5 days or 30 days community service (second); 10 days or 60 days community service (third); mandatory fine
notes: Second DWI within 10 years: 1-year minimum license revocation. Third within 10 years: 1-year minimum revocation. Ignition interlock required. Permanent revocation possible for multiple felony DWIs.

statute_title: Driving While Ability Impaired by Drugs (DWAI-Drugs)
offense_class: Unclassified Misdemeanor (first); Class E Felony (second within 10 years); Class D Felony (third within 10 years)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
While ability was impaired by the use of a drug as defined in Public Health Law § 3302
Impairment to a degree that rendered the defendant incapable of operating the vehicle safely
mandatory_minimum: Same structure as alcohol DWI by offense count
enhancements: Combined influence of alcohol and drugs (§ 1192(4-a))
notes: DWAI-Drugs carries the same penalties as per se DWI. Drug Recognition Expert evaluations commonly used. Includes prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, and controlled substances.

offense_class: Unclassified Misdemeanor (first); Unclassified Misdemeanor with enhanced penalties (second+)
penalty_max: 30 days (first); 90 days (second within 18 months); 180 days (third within 18 months)
elements: Defendant drove or used a motor vehicle or motorcycle
In a manner which unreasonably interfered with the free and proper use of the public highway
Or unreasonably endangered users of the public highway
enhancements: Third offense within 18 months (further enhanced penalties)
notes: Common plea-down from DWI. 5 points on driving record. Enhanced penalties for repeat offenses within 18 months.

statute_title: Leaving the Scene of an Incident
offense_class: Class E Felony (serious physical injury); Class D Felony (death); Class A Misdemeanor (personal injury); Traffic Infraction (property damage)
penalty_max: 4 years (serious injury); 7 years (death); 1 year (personal injury); 15 days (property damage)
elements: Defendant was the operator of a vehicle involved in an accident
Accident resulted in injury, death, or property damage
Defendant failed to stop, exhibit license and registration, and provide insurance information
Defendant failed to render reasonable assistance
notes: New York grades leaving the scene by the severity of the result. Property damage only is a traffic infraction. Personal injury is a Class A Misdemeanor. Serious injury or death are felonies.

offense_class: Class D Felony
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle while intoxicated
And caused the death of another person
While DWI was a contributing factor in the death
enhancements: First-degree vehicular manslaughter (§ 125.13 — Class C Felony if multiple deaths or BAC .18+, up to 15 years)
Suspended license at time of incident
notes: Vehicular manslaughter second degree is a Class D Felony. First-degree vehicular manslaughter (§ 125.13) applies when BAC is .18+, license was suspended for DWI, or multiple deaths occur — Class C Felony up to 15 years.

offense_class: Class D Felony
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle while intoxicated or impaired
And caused the death of another person
Or defendant drove in a criminally negligent manner and caused the death of another
enhancements: First degree vehicular manslaughter (§ 125.13 — Class C Felony, up to 15 years)
notes: Covers both DWI-related deaths and criminally negligent driving deaths. First degree applies to aggravated circumstances.

statute_title: Operation While License Suspended or Revoked
offense_class: Unclassified Misdemeanor (first, non-DWI suspension); Class E Felony (DWI-related suspension, third+ within 10 years, or knowing/willful)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle upon a public highway
While knowing or having reason to know that their license was suspended or revoked
mandatory_minimum: Mandatory fine; possible mandatory jail for repeat offenders
enhancements: Driving during DWI-related suspension (Aggravated Unlicensed Operation — AUO 1st degree, Class E Felony under § 511(3))
Operating while under the influence during suspension (enhanced)
notes: New York uses Aggravated Unlicensed Operation (AUO) with three degrees. AUO 3rd degree: Unclassified Misdemeanor. AUO 2nd degree: Unclassified Misdemeanor with mandatory fine. AUO 1st degree: Class E Felony.

statute_number: N.Y. Veh. & Traf. Law § 1102 / N.Y. Penal Law § 270.25
statute_title: Failure to Comply with Officer's Direction / Unlawful Fleeing a Police Officer
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (unlawful fleeing); Traffic Infraction (failure to comply)
elements: A police officer directed the defendant to stop
Defendant, knowing they were directed to stop by a police officer
Fled in a motor vehicle
And engaged in conduct that created a substantial risk of serious physical injury
enhancements: Creating substantial risk of serious physical injury
notes: Unlawful fleeing a police officer (Penal Law § 270.25) is a Class A Misdemeanor. Simple failure to comply with an officer's direction (VTL § 1102) is a traffic infraction.

statute_title: Criminal Possession of a Controlled Substance — Seventh Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant knowingly and unlawfully possessed a controlled substance
Substance is listed on New York controlled substance schedules
enhancements: Possession of larger quantities (elevated degrees — up to Class A-I Felony)
notes: Seventh degree is the lowest-level drug possession. New York has seven degrees of criminal possession of a controlled substance, from Class A Misdemeanor (7th) to Class A-I Felony (1st). Drug court and diversion widely available.

statute_title: Unlawful Possession of Cannabis — Second Degree
offense_class: Violation (≤3 oz or 24g concentrate); Class A Misdemeanor (>3 oz); Class E Felony (>16 oz)
penalty_max: $50 fine (≤3 oz first); 1 year (>3 oz misdemeanor); 4 years (>16 oz felony)
elements: Defendant possessed cannabis in excess of legally permitted amounts
Adults 21+: 3 oz flower / 24g concentrate is legal limit
enhancements: More than 16 ounces (Class E Felony under § 222.30)
More than 5 pounds (Class D Felony under § 222.35)
notes: New York legalized recreational cannabis in 2021 (MRTA). Adults 21+ may possess up to 3 oz flower or 24g concentrate. Exceeding legal limits is criminal. Under-21 possession remains illegal.

statute_title: Criminal Possession of a Controlled Substance — Fifth Degree (Cocaine)
offense_class: Class D Felony (≥500mg); Class A Misdemeanor (small amount under § 220.03)
penalty_max: 7 years (Class D Felony); 1 year (Class A Misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant knowingly and unlawfully possessed cocaine
In an aggregate weight of 500 milligrams or more (for 5th degree)
Cocaine is a Schedule II controlled substance in New York
enhancements: Possession of ≥1/2 oz (4th degree — Class C Felony)
Possession of ≥4 oz (2nd degree — Class A-II Felony)
Possession of ≥8 oz (1st degree — Class A-I Felony, 15–25 years to life)
notes: New York grades cocaine possession by weight. 500mg triggers Class D Felony. 1/2 oz triggers Class C Felony. The most severe (8+ oz) carries 15–25 years to life.

statute_title: Criminal Possession of Methamphetamine — Fifth Degree
offense_class: Class D Felony
elements: Defendant knowingly and unlawfully possessed methamphetamine
Methamphetamine is a Schedule II controlled substance
In an amount triggering fifth degree possession
notes: Methamphetamine possession is prosecuted under the general controlled substance statutes. Quantity determines the degree of the offense.

statute_title: Criminal Sale of a Controlled Substance — First Degree
offense_class: Class A-I Felony (1st degree); Class A-II Felony (2nd degree); Class B Felony (3rd degree)
penalty_min: 8 years (Class A-I); 3 years (Class A-II); 1 year (Class B)
penalty_max: Life (Class A-I); Life (Class A-II); 25 years (Class B)
fine_max: $100,000 or double the profit (Class A-I); $50,000 (Class A-II); $30,000 (Class B)
elements: Defendant knowingly and unlawfully sold a controlled substance
The substance was a narcotic drug or other controlled substance
Quantity or circumstances met the threshold for the specific degree
mandatory_minimum: 8 years (1st degree); 3 years (2nd degree); 1 year (3rd degree)
enhancements: Sale near a school (§ 220.44 — Class B Felony)
Major trafficker provisions (§ 220.77 — Class A-I Felony)
notes: New York has five degrees of criminal sale of a controlled substance. Major trafficker statute (§ 220.77) applies to leaders of drug organizations. Penalties were modified by the Drug Law Reform Act of 2009.

statute_title: Criminal Sale of a Controlled Substance — Third Degree
offense_class: Class B Felony
elements: Defendant knowingly and unlawfully sold a controlled substance
To another person
notes: Third-degree sale is the baseline drug sale offense. Covers any sale of a narcotic drug or controlled substance regardless of quantity.

offense_class: Class D Felony (3rd degree); Class B Felony (1st degree — child present or prior conviction)
elements: Defendant possessed precursor chemicals, equipment, or reagents
With intent to manufacture methamphetamine
Or defendant engaged in the manufacturing process
enhancements: Child present during manufacturing (1st degree — Class B Felony under § 220.74)
notes: New York has specific methamphetamine manufacturing statutes (§ 220.71–220.77). General drug manufacturing is prosecuted under possession and sale statutes.

statute_title: Criminally Using Drug Paraphernalia — Second Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed or sold drug paraphernalia
With knowledge of its nature and intent that it be used to prepare or administer controlled substances
enhancements: Sale of drug paraphernalia (first degree — Class D Felony under § 220.55 if commercially)
notes: Possession of paraphernalia is a Class A Misdemeanor. Commercial sale of drug paraphernalia is more serious. New York has harm reduction exemptions for syringe possession.

statute_title: Criminal Possession of a Controlled Substance — Third Degree (Intent to Sell)
offense_class: Class B Felony
elements: Defendant knowingly and unlawfully possessed a controlled substance
With intent to sell it
Narcotic drug or stimulant in specified amounts
notes: Third-degree possession with intent to sell is a Class B Felony. Intent can be inferred from quantity, packaging, scales, and other evidence.

offense_class: Class A-I Felony
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause the death of another person, caused the death of such person
Under one of the aggravating circumstances specified in the statute
Including murder of a police officer, judge, witness, during a robbery, kidnapping, or sexual offense, or by contract
mandatory_minimum: 20 years to life (minimum); Life without parole (maximum)
enhancements: Murder of a police officer or peace officer
notes: New York does not have the death penalty (declared unconstitutional 2004, governor's moratorium since 2007). First-degree murder requires specific aggravating circumstances. Sentence is life without parole or 20–25 years to life.

offense_class: Class A-I Felony
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause the death of another person, caused the death of such person
Or under circumstances evincing a depraved indifference to human life, recklessly engaged in conduct creating a grave risk of death and thereby caused death
Or during commission of specified felonies (felony murder)
enhancements: Felony murder (during robbery, burglary, kidnapping, arson, rape, etc.)
Prior violent felony conviction (25 years to life minimum)
notes: Second-degree murder is the most commonly charged murder offense in New York. Covers intentional murder, depraved indifference murder, and felony murder. Mandatory indeterminate sentence of 15–25 years to life.

offense_class: Class B Felony
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause serious physical injury to another, caused the death of such person
Or caused the death under circumstances which do not constitute murder because of extreme emotional disturbance
An affirmative defense partially reducing murder to manslaughter
notes: First-degree manslaughter includes intent to cause serious injury resulting in death, and the extreme emotional disturbance defense to murder. It is a Class B Felony.

offense_class: Class C Felony
elements: Defendant recklessly caused the death of another person
notes: Second-degree manslaughter covers reckless killings. Does not require intent to kill or injure — only that defendant was aware of and disregarded a substantial risk.

offense_class: Class B Felony
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause serious physical injury, caused serious physical injury by means of a deadly weapon or dangerous instrument
Or with intent to disfigure seriously and permanently, or destroy, amputate, or disable a member or organ, caused such injury
Or recklessly caused serious physical injury by means of a deadly weapon under circumstances evincing depraved indifference to human life
enhancements: Against a police officer or peace officer (§ 120.11 — Class B violent felony)
notes: First-degree assault is a violent Class B Felony. Serious physical injury means injury creating a substantial risk of death or causing permanent disfigurement, protracted health impairment, or loss of organ function.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause physical injury to another, caused such injury
Or recklessly caused physical injury to another
Or with criminal negligence caused physical injury by means of a deadly weapon or dangerous instrument
enhancements: Against certain protected persons (elevated to second degree)
notes: Third-degree assault is the basic assault offense in New York. Physical injury means impairment of physical condition or substantial pain.

statute_title: Assault in the Third Degree (Battery Equivalent)
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant intentionally caused physical injury to another person
Through physical contact
notes: New York does not have a separate battery statute. What other states call battery is prosecuted as third-degree assault.

offense_class: Class D Felony
elements: Defendant forcibly stole property
By using or threatening the immediate use of physical force upon another person
enhancements: Aided by another (2nd degree — Class C Felony under § 160.10)
Armed with deadly weapon (1st degree — Class B Felony under § 160.15)
notes: New York has three degrees of robbery. Third degree: basic forcible stealing (Class D). Second degree: aided by another or causing injury (Class C). First degree: armed with weapon, causing serious injury, or displaying a firearm (Class B).

offense_class: Class B Felony
elements: Defendant forcibly stole property
And was armed with a deadly weapon
Or used or threatened the immediate use of a dangerous instrument
Or caused serious physical injury to a non-participant
enhancements: Display of a firearm (always first degree)
Serious physical injury to any non-participant
notes: First-degree robbery is a violent Class B Felony. Mandatory minimum 5 years determinate sentence. Display of what appears to be a firearm is sufficient.

offense_class: Class B Felony (2nd degree); Class A-I Felony (1st degree — ransom or not released)
penalty_min: 5 years (2nd degree); 20 years to life (1st degree)
elements: Defendant abducted another person
Restrained the person with intent to prevent liberation
By secreting or holding in a place of isolation, or by threat of use of deadly physical force
enhancements: For ransom (1st degree — Class A-I under § 135.25)
notes: Second-degree kidnapping is the basic offense (Class B Felony). First degree applies when kidnapping is for ransom, involves a third-party threat, or victim is not safely returned.

offense_class: Class B Felony (2nd degree — building); Class A-I Felony (1st degree — person in building and explosive device)
elements: Defendant intentionally damaged a building or motor vehicle by starting a fire or causing an explosion
enhancements: Person present in building with explosive device (1st degree — Class A-I under § 150.20)
notes: New York has five degrees of arson. Fifth degree: reckless property damage (Class A Misdemeanor). Fourth degree: property damage over $250 (Class E Felony). Third degree: building damage (Class C Felony). Second degree: building intentionally damaged (Class B Felony). First degree: explosive + person present (Class A-I).

statute_title: Attempted Murder in the Second Degree
offense_class: Class B Felony
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause the death of another person
Engaged in conduct that tended to effect the commission of murder
But was unsuccessful in causing death
enhancements: Attempted murder of a police officer
notes: Attempted murder in the second degree is a Class B violent felony. Attempt reduces the grade by one level from the completed offense (A-I to B).

statute_title: Assault in the Second Degree — Deadly Weapon
offense_class: Class D Felony
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause physical injury to another person
Caused such injury by means of a deadly weapon or dangerous instrument
enhancements: Serious physical injury (elevated to first degree — Class B Felony)
notes: Second-degree assault with a deadly weapon is a Class D Felony. If serious physical injury results, it becomes first-degree assault (Class B Felony).

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (petit — ≤$1,000); Class E Felony (4th degree — >$1,000); Class D Felony (3rd degree — >$3,000); Class C Felony (2nd degree — >$50,000); Class B Felony (1st degree — >$1M)
penalty_max: 1 year (misdemeanor); 4 years (4th degree); 7 years (3rd degree); 15 years (2nd degree); 25 years (1st degree)
elements: Defendant stole property
With intent to deprive the owner or to appropriate the property to self or a third person
enhancements: Theft from a person (always 4th degree minimum)
notes: New York has one of the most detailed theft grading systems. Petit larceny (≤$1,000) is Class A Misdemeanor. Grand larceny 4th degree (>$1,000) through 1st degree (>$1M) are felonies.

statute_title: Grand Larceny in the Fourth Degree
offense_class: Class E Felony (4th — >$1,000); Class D Felony (3rd — >$3,000); Class C Felony (2nd — >$50,000); Class B Felony (1st — >$1M)
elements: Defendant stole property
Value exceeding $1,000
notes: Grand larceny begins at property value exceeding $1,000. Also applies regardless of value when theft is from a person, ATM skimming, or theft of certain items (firearms, religious items, etc.).

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant stole property
Value was $1,000 or less
notes: Petit larceny covers all theft of property valued at $1,000 or less (unless aggravating factors apply). Class A Misdemeanor.

statute_title: Petit Larceny / Criminal Possession of Stolen Property — Shoplifting
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (≤$1,000); Class E Felony (>$1,000)
elements: Defendant took merchandise from a retail establishment
Without paying the purchase price
With intent to deprive the merchant
enhancements: Anti-shoplifting device defeat tools (§ 170.45 — Class A Misdemeanor)
notes: New York prosecutes shoplifting primarily under petit larceny or grand larceny. Possession of anti-security tags is a separate offense.

offense_class: Class D Felony (3rd degree); Class C Felony (2nd degree); Class B Felony (1st degree)
elements: Defendant knowingly entered or remained unlawfully in a building
With intent to commit a crime therein
enhancements: Building is a dwelling (2nd degree — Class C under § 140.25)
Armed with explosive or deadly weapon (1st degree — Class B under § 140.30)
notes: Three degrees of burglary. Third degree: any building (Class D). Second degree: dwelling (Class C — violent felony). First degree: armed, causes injury, or displays firearm (Class B — violent felony).

offense_class: Class C Felony (violent felony)
elements: Defendant knowingly entered or remained unlawfully in a building
With intent to commit a crime therein
The building was a dwelling
enhancements: Armed during burglary (elevated to 1st degree — Class B)
notes: Dwelling means any building used for lodging of persons overnight. Second-degree burglary is a violent felony with mandatory minimum sentence.

offense_class: Class E Felony (4th degree — motor vehicle regardless of value)
elements: Defendant stole a motor vehicle
As defined in Vehicle and Traffic Law
enhancements: Vehicle value exceeds $3,000 (3rd degree — Class D Felony)
notes: Motor vehicle theft is always at least grand larceny in the fourth degree (Class E Felony) regardless of vehicle value.

statute_title: Criminal Possession of Stolen Property — Fifth Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (5th degree); Class E Felony (4th degree — >$1,000); Class D Felony (3rd degree — >$3,000); Class C Felony (2nd degree — >$50,000); Class B Felony (1st degree — >$1M)
penalty_max: 1 year (misdemeanor); up to 25 years (1st degree felony)
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed stolen property
With intent to benefit self or a person other than the owner
enhancements: Value thresholds (same grading as grand larceny)
notes: Five degrees of criminal possession of stolen property, graded by value. Same thresholds as larceny.

statute_title: Criminal Mischief in the Fourth Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (4th degree); Class E Felony (3rd degree — >$250); Class D Felony (2nd degree — >$1,500); Class B Felony (1st degree — explosive)
elements: Defendant, having no right to do so or any reasonable ground to believe they had such right
Intentionally damaged property of another person
enhancements: Damage exceeding $250 (3rd degree — Class E Felony)
Damage exceeding $1,500 (2nd degree — Class D Felony)
Use of explosive (1st degree — Class B Felony)
notes: Four degrees of criminal mischief. Graded by damage amount and method. Use of explosives is first degree (Class B Felony).

offense_class: Violation (basic under § 140.05); Class B Misdemeanor (3rd degree — fenced/enclosed under § 140.10); Class A Misdemeanor (2nd degree — dwelling under § 140.15)
elements: Defendant knowingly entered or remained unlawfully in or upon premises
enhancements: Fenced or enclosed premises (3rd degree — Class B Misdemeanor)
notes: Basic trespass is a violation. Third degree applies to fenced or enclosed premises. Second degree applies to dwellings. Trespass in a dwelling is a precursor to burglary charges if intent to commit a crime exists.

statute_title: Criminal Mischief in the Fourth Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (4th); up to Class B Felony (1st)
elements: Defendant intentionally damaged property of another having no right to do so
Or recklessly damaged property in an amount exceeding $250
notes: Same statute as vandalism. Four degrees based on damage amount and method.

statute_number: N.Y. Penal Law § 120.00 / § 240.26 / Family Court Act § 812
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (3rd degree assault); Class E Felony (2nd degree); Class B Felony (1st degree); Class B Misdemeanor (harassment)
penalty_max: 1 year (misdemeanor); up to 25 years (1st degree assault)
elements: Defendant committed an assault, menacing, harassment, stalking, or other designated offense
Against a family or household member
Family or household member includes spouse, former spouse, persons related by blood or marriage, persons in intimate relationship, parent of shared child
enhancements: Strangulation (1st or 2nd degree — Class C or D Felony under § 121.11–121.12)
Criminal contempt for violating order of protection
notes: New York does not have a standalone 'domestic violence' charge. DV is prosecuted under existing assault, harassment, menacing, and stalking statutes with the domestic relationship as context. Strangulation statutes (§ 121.11–121.13) were added specifically for DV cases.

statute_title: Assault in the Third Degree — Domestic Context
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant intentionally caused physical injury to a family or household member
First offense
enhancements: Use of a weapon (elevated to 2nd degree assault)
Serious physical injury (elevated to 1st degree assault)
notes: No separate domestic battery charge in New York. Prosecuted as third-degree assault with domestic relationship noted. Batterer intervention program commonly ordered.

statute_title: Endangering the Welfare of a Child
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant knowingly acted in a manner likely to be injurious to the physical, mental, or moral welfare of a child under 17
Or directed or authorized such child to engage in an occupation harmful to the child's health
enhancements: DUI with child in vehicle (Leandra's Law — felony)
notes: Broadly worded statute covering a wide range of conduct endangering children. Commonly charged alongside DWI (Leandra's Law), drug offenses, and domestic violence.

statute_title: Assault on a Child / Endangering Welfare
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (endangering welfare); Class D Felony (assault 2nd on child under 11 under § 120.05(8)); higher for serious injury
elements: Defendant caused physical injury to a child
Being a person over 18 and the child being under 11 (for 2nd degree assault)
Or defendant caused serious physical injury to a child
enhancements: Serious physical injury (1st degree assault — Class B Felony)
Child under 11 (assault 2nd — Class D Felony under § 120.05(8))
notes: Child abuse is prosecuted under assault statutes (with age enhancement for children under 11) and the endangering welfare statute. ACS involvement accompanies criminal prosecution in NYC.

statute_title: Criminal Contempt in the First Degree (Violation of Order of Protection)
offense_class: Class E Felony (1st degree); Class A Misdemeanor (2nd degree under § 215.50)
penalty_max: 4 years (1st degree — Class E Felony); 1 year (2nd degree)
elements: A valid order of protection was in effect
Defendant had knowledge of the order
Defendant intentionally or knowingly violated the order
And placed the protected person in reasonable fear of physical injury (for 1st degree)
enhancements: Aggravated criminal contempt (§ 215.52 — Class D Felony if physical injury caused)
notes: Criminal contempt in the first degree (Class E Felony) applies when violation places person in reasonable fear of injury. Aggravated criminal contempt (Class D Felony) applies when physical injury is actually caused.

offense_class: Class B Misdemeanor (4th degree); Class A Misdemeanor (3rd degree under § 120.50); Class E Felony (2nd degree under § 120.55); Class D Felony (1st degree under § 120.60)
elements: Defendant intentionally and for no legitimate purpose engaged in a course of conduct directed at a specific person
That was likely to cause reasonable fear of material harm to the health, safety, or property of such person
enhancements: Commission of enumerated sex offense during course of conduct (2nd degree)
Threat of physical injury and prior conviction for stalking or specified crime against same victim (1st degree)
notes: New York has four degrees of stalking. Fourth degree is the baseline. First degree requires a threat of physical injury plus a prior conviction for a specified crime against the same victim.

offense_class: Violation (2nd degree); Class A Misdemeanor (1st degree — physical contact under § 240.25); Class B Misdemeanor (aggravated under § 240.30)
elements: Defendant, with intent to harass, annoy, or alarm another person
Struck, shoved, kicked, or otherwise subjected to physical contact
Or followed a person in or about a public place
Or engaged in a course of conduct serving no legitimate purpose which alarmed or seriously annoyed the person
enhancements: Physical contact (1st degree — Class A Misdemeanor)
Aggravated harassment by electronic means (§ 240.30 — Class B Misdemeanor)
notes: Second-degree harassment is a violation (non-criminal). First-degree harassment involves physical contact (Class A Misdemeanor). Aggravated harassment includes electronic/telephone threats.

statute_title: Endangering the Welfare of a Vulnerable Elderly Person
offense_class: Class E Felony (2nd degree); Class D Felony (1st degree — involving physical injury)
elements: Defendant knowingly or recklessly caused physical injury or financial exploitation
To a person 60 years of age or older who was vulnerable or incapacitated
Defendant was a caregiver or person responsible for the elder's care
enhancements: Physical injury (1st degree — Class D Felony under § 260.34)
notes: New York enacted specific elder abuse statutes (§ 260.32–260.34). Adult Protective Services investigates. Covers both physical abuse and financial exploitation.

statute_title: Criminal Possession of a Weapon — Fourth Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (4th degree); Class D Felony (3rd degree under § 265.02); Class C Felony (2nd degree under § 265.03); Class B Felony (1st degree under § 265.04)
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm, dangerous knife, or other prohibited weapon
Without a valid license or permit
mandatory_minimum: 3.5 years (2nd degree loaded firearm — violent felony)
enhancements: Loaded firearm (2nd degree — Class C violent felony under § 265.03)
Prior conviction + any firearm (3rd degree — Class D under § 265.02)
Possession of 10+ firearms (1st degree — Class B under § 265.04)
notes: New York has extremely strict weapons laws. Possession of a loaded firearm outside home/place of business without a permit is a Class C violent felony with a 3.5-year mandatory minimum. Four degrees of criminal possession of a weapon.

statute_title: Criminal Possession of a Weapon — Third Degree (Prior Conviction)
offense_class: Class D Felony
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm or other weapon
Defendant had been previously convicted of any crime
enhancements: Loaded firearm (elevated to 2nd degree — Class C violent felony)
notes: Any prior conviction (not just felonies) elevates weapon possession to third degree (Class D Felony). New York's weapons laws are among the strictest in the nation.

statute_title: Criminal Possession of a Firearm — Sensitive Location
offense_class: Class E Felony
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm, rifle, or shotgun
In a sensitive location or restricted location as defined by law
Including schools, government buildings, houses of worship, subways, Times Square, etc.
notes: After the NYSRPA v. Bruen Supreme Court decision, New York enacted the Concealed Carry Improvement Act (2022) establishing sensitive and restricted locations where carry is prohibited even with a permit.

statute_title: Prohibited Use of Weapons — Reckless Discharge
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (general); Felony (if endangering persons in specific ways)
elements: Defendant discharged a firearm
In a manner that endangered the safety of another
Or discharged in a populated area
enhancements: Discharge from or at a motor vehicle
notes: Reckless discharge is prosecuted under prohibited use of weapons or reckless endangerment statutes. In NYC, additional city ordinances apply.

statute_title: Identity Theft in the Third Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (3rd degree); Class E Felony (2nd degree under § 190.79); Class D Felony (1st degree under § 190.80)
elements: Defendant knowingly and with intent to defraud assumed the identity of another
By using personal identifying information of that person
To obtain goods, money, property, services, or to commit a crime
enhancements: Value exceeding $500 (2nd degree — Class E Felony)
Value exceeding $2,000 (1st degree — Class D Felony)
Victim is a member of the armed forces serving abroad
notes: Three degrees of identity theft graded by value. New York also has aggravated identity theft (§ 190.80-a — Class D Felony) for identity theft targeting specific vulnerable populations.

offense_class: Same grading as larceny by value
elements: Defendant was entrusted with property of another
Defendant wrongfully took, obtained, or withheld the property
By exercising unauthorized control over the property
notes: New York prosecutes embezzlement as a form of larceny. Graded by the same value thresholds.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (3rd); Class D Felony (2nd under § 170.10); Class C Felony (1st under § 170.15)
elements: Defendant falsely made, completed, or altered a written instrument
With intent to defraud, deceive, or injure another
enhancements: Deed, will, contract, government document (2nd degree — Class D Felony)
Money, stamps, securities (1st degree — Class C Felony)
notes: Three degrees of forgery. Third: any instrument (Class A Misdemeanor). Second: deeds, wills, contracts, government documents (Class D Felony). First: money, stamps, securities (Class C Felony).

offense_class: Class C Felony
elements: Defendant falsely made, completed, or altered currency, stamps, or securities
With intent to defraud
notes: First-degree forgery covers counterfeiting of currency, stamps, and securities. Federal counterfeiting charges typically also apply.

offense_class: Class B Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant issued a check knowing there were insufficient funds
And payment was refused by the drawee
Defendant failed to make good within 10 days of receiving notice of dishonor
notes: Issuing a bad check is a Class B Misdemeanor. More serious cases may be prosecuted as larceny by false promise or scheme to defraud.

statute_title: Insurance Fraud in the Fourth Degree
offense_class: Class E Felony (4th degree — >$1,000); Class D Felony (3rd degree — >$3,000); Class C Felony (2nd degree — >$50,000); Class B Felony (1st degree — >$1M)
elements: Defendant, in the course of committing an insurance fraud act
Knowingly and with intent to defraud presented a false or fraudulent claim for insurance benefits
Value exceeding the applicable threshold
notes: Five degrees of insurance fraud. Fifth degree (under $1,000) is a Class A Misdemeanor. Graded up to first degree (over $1M) which is a Class B Felony.

statute_title: Grand Larceny / Scheme to Defraud — Credit Card
offense_class: Class E Felony (basic >$1,000); Higher degrees by value
penalty_max: 4 years (Class E); up to 25 years (Class B for very large amounts)
elements: Defendant used a credit card, debit card, or account number of another
Without the cardholder's authorization
To obtain goods, services, or anything of value
notes: Credit card fraud is prosecuted as larceny, identity theft, or scheme to defraud depending on circumstances and amount.

statute_title: Money Laundering in the Fourth Degree
offense_class: Class E Felony (4th — >$5,000); Class D Felony (3rd — >$50,000); Class C Felony (2nd — >$100,000); Class B Felony (1st — >$500,000)
fine_max: $5,000 or twice the value of laundered funds
elements: Defendant conducted or attempted to conduct a financial transaction
Involving proceeds of specified criminal conduct
Knowing that the property represented proceeds of some form of criminal conduct
notes: Four degrees of money laundering graded by the amount involved. Fine may be up to twice the value of the laundered funds.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (2nd degree); Class E Felony (1st degree — >$1,000 from 1+ persons under § 190.65)
elements: Defendant engaged in a scheme constituting a systematic ongoing course of conduct
With intent to defraud 10+ persons or one person of >$1,000
By false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises
enhancements: 1st degree — value exceeding $1,000 from one or more persons (Class E Felony)
notes: New York's general fraud statute. Second degree requires scheme affecting 10+ persons. First degree requires obtaining >$1,000 from one or more persons.

statute_title: Criminal Sexual Act in the First Degree
offense_class: Class B Felony (1st degree — forcible); Class D Felony (2nd degree under § 130.45); Class E Felony (3rd degree under § 130.40)
elements: Defendant engaged in oral or anal sexual conduct with another person
By forcible compulsion
Or the person was incapable of consent due to being physically helpless, mentally disabled, or under a specified age
enhancements: Victim under 13 (1st degree — Class B violent felony)
notes: Criminal sexual act covers oral and anal sexual conduct. Rape statute (§ 130.35) covers vaginal intercourse. Three degrees based on force, age, and incapacity.

offense_class: Class B Felony (1st degree); Class D Felony (2nd degree under § 130.30); Class E Felony (3rd degree under § 130.25)
elements: Defendant engaged in sexual intercourse with another person
By forcible compulsion (1st degree)
Or with a person who was incapable of consent due to being physically helpless (1st degree)
Or who was under 11 years of age (1st degree)
enhancements: Victim under 11 (1st degree — Class B violent felony)
notes: Three degrees of rape. First: forcible compulsion, physically helpless, or under 11 (Class B violent felony). Second: under 15 (Class D). Third: under 17 and defendant 21+, or incapacity (Class E). Statute of limitations eliminated for 1st degree rape.

statute_title: Public Lewdness / Exposure of a Person
offense_class: Class B Misdemeanor (public lewdness); Class A Misdemeanor (exposure of a person — child present under § 245.02)
penalty_max: 3 months (Class B); 1 year (Class A if child present)
elements: Defendant intentionally exposed private or intimate parts of the body
In a lewd manner
In a public place
notes: Public lewdness is a Class B Misdemeanor. Exposure of a person (intentional exposure to child under 14) is a Class A Misdemeanor.

statute_title: Patronizing a Person for Prostitution — Third Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (3rd degree — adult); Class E Felony (2nd degree — under 14 under § 230.05); Class D Felony (1st degree — under 11 under § 230.06)
elements: Defendant patronized a person for prostitution
By paying or agreeing to pay a fee in return for sexual conduct
enhancements: Victim under 14 (2nd degree — Class E Felony)
Victim under 11 (1st degree — Class D Felony)
notes: New York focuses enforcement on buyers (patrons) rather than sellers. Prostitution itself (§ 230.00) is a Class B Misdemeanor. Sex trafficking charges apply when force or minors are involved.

statute_title: Possessing / Promoting a Sexual Performance by a Child
offense_class: Class E Felony (possession under § 263.16); Class D Felony (promoting under § 263.10); Class C Felony (production under § 263.05)
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed or promoted a sexual performance by a child under 16
Or defendant used, caused, or allowed a child under 16 to engage in a sexual performance
notes: Possession is a Class E Felony. Promoting (distributing) is a Class D Felony. Producing/directing is a Class C Felony. Each image may constitute a separate count.

statute_title: Failure to Register or Verify as Sex Offender (SORA)
offense_class: Class E Felony (first); Class D Felony (second+)
elements: Defendant was required to register under the Sex Offender Registration Act (SORA)
Defendant knowingly failed to register, verify, or update registration
Or provided false information
enhancements: Second or subsequent failure to register (Class D Felony)
notes: SORA registration required for 20 years (Level 1), life (Level 2), or life (Level 3). Level 3 offenders must verify every 90 days.

offense_class: Class E Felony (3rd degree — under 17 and defendant 21+); Class D Felony (2nd degree — under 15); Class B Felony (1st degree — under 11)
elements: Defendant engaged in sexual intercourse with a person under the age of consent
Defendant was of a specified age making consent irrelevant
Third degree: victim under 17, defendant 21+; Second degree: victim under 15; First degree: victim under 11
enhancements: Victim under 11 (1st degree — Class B violent felony)
notes: New York age of consent is 17. Third-degree rape applies when victim is under 17 and defendant is 21+. Second degree applies when victim is under 15. First degree when victim is under 11 or forcible compulsion.

offense_class: Violation
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause public inconvenience, annoyance, or alarm
Or recklessly creating a risk thereof
Engaged in fighting, violent or threatening behavior, unreasonable noise, obscene language in public, or obstructing traffic
notes: Disorderly conduct is a violation (not a crime) in New York. Maximum 15 days jail. Very commonly used as a plea-down from misdemeanor charges.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant intentionally prevented or attempted to prevent a police officer or peace officer
From effecting an authorized arrest
By means of physical force or other means creating a substantial risk of physical injury
notes: Requires physical force or creation of substantial risk of injury. Applies regardless of whether the underlying arrest was ultimately valid.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant intentionally obstructed, impaired, or perverted the administration of law
Or other governmental function
By means of intimidation, physical force, or interference
notes: Broader than resisting arrest. Covers interference with any governmental function. Includes providing false information to law enforcement.

statute_title: Criminal Contempt in the Second Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (2nd degree); Class E Felony (1st degree under § 215.51); Class D Felony (aggravated under § 215.52)
elements: Defendant engaged in disorderly conduct in the court's presence
Or intentionally disobeyed a lawful mandate of the court
Or violated an order of protection
enhancements: Violation of order of protection placing person in fear (1st degree — Class E Felony)
Violation causing physical injury (aggravated — Class D Felony)
notes: Three levels of criminal contempt. Most commonly used for violation of orders of protection. Aggravated criminal contempt (Class D Felony) applies when physical injury is caused during violation.

offense_class: Not a criminal offense in most circumstances
elements: Person is found in a public place in an intoxicated condition
And is a danger to self or others
notes: New York does not have a public intoxication criminal statute. Intoxicated persons may be taken into protective custody. Disorderly conduct may be charged if conduct meets those elements.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (underlying is misdemeanor); Class E Felony (underlying Class A-E Felony); Class D Felony (underlying Class A-B Felony)
elements: Defendant was released from custody on bail or recognizance
For a pending criminal action
Defendant did not appear on the required day in court
notes: Three degrees of bail jumping based on seriousness of underlying charge. Court issues bench warrant.

statute_title: Falsely Reporting an Incident — Third Degree
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (3rd degree); Class D Felony (1st degree — if causes death under § 240.60); Class E Felony (2nd degree under § 240.55)
elements: Defendant reported an alleged offense or incident to a law enforcement agency or emergency service
Knowing the information to be false
enhancements: False report of a bomb or biological/chemical weapon (2nd degree — Class E Felony)
False report causing death (1st degree — Class D Felony)
notes: Three degrees of falsely reporting an incident. Bomb threats and biological weapon hoaxes are second degree felonies.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (2nd degree); Class E Felony (1st degree — deadly weapon under § 120.18); Class B Misdemeanor (3rd degree under § 120.15)
penalty_max: 1 year (2nd degree); 4 years (1st degree); 3 months (3rd degree)
elements: Defendant intentionally placed or attempted to place another person in fear of physical injury
By displaying a weapon or dangerous instrument
Or through repeated conduct or threats
enhancements: Display of a deadly weapon (1st degree — Class E Felony under § 120.18)
Repeated threatening conduct toward same person
notes: New York uses 'menacing' for criminal threats. Three degrees based on severity. First degree (weapon display) is a Class E Felony.

offense_class: Class E Felony (2nd degree); Class D Felony (1st degree under § 210.15)
elements: Defendant made a false statement under oath
In a proceeding or matter in which the oath was required by law
The false statement was material to the proceeding
enhancements: Perjury in a proceeding (1st degree — material false statement in a subscribed written instrument)
notes: Two degrees of perjury. Second degree: false sworn statement in any proceeding. First degree: false statement in a subscribed written instrument known to be material.

offense_class: Class D Felony (3rd degree); Class C Felony (2nd degree under § 200.03); Class B Felony (1st degree under § 200.04)
fine_max: $5,000 or double the value of the bribe
elements: Defendant conferred or offered to confer any benefit upon a public servant
As consideration for the public servant's vote, opinion, judgment, action, decision, or exercise of discretion
notes: Three degrees of bribery graded by value. Both offering and accepting bribes are criminal offenses.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (3rd degree); Class E Felony (2nd degree under § 205.10); Class D Felony (1st degree under § 205.15)
elements: Defendant was in custody or detention
Defendant escaped from such custody
Without permission of the appropriate authority
enhancements: Use of a dangerous instrument (2nd degree — Class E Felony)
Use of a deadly weapon (1st degree — Class D Felony)
notes: Three degrees of escape. Third: basic escape (Class A Misdemeanor). Second: using a dangerous instrument (Class E Felony). First: using a deadly weapon or dangerous instrument causing injury (Class D Felony).

statute_title: Overdriving, Torturing, and Injuring Animals / Failure to Provide Sustenance
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (general under § 353); Class E Felony (aggravated under § 353-a)
elements: Defendant overdrove, overloaded, tortured, cruelly beat, or unjustifiably injured an animal
Or failed to provide necessary sustenance
Whether the animal belongs to the defendant or another
enhancements: Aggravated cruelty — intentional killing or torture causing extreme physical suffering (Class E Felony under § 353-a)
notes: General animal cruelty is a Class A Misdemeanor under Agriculture & Markets Law. Aggravated cruelty (intentional torture) is a Class E Felony. Animal fighting is separately criminalized.

offense_class: Depends on underlying offense
elements: Defendant was placed on probation
Defendant violated a condition of probation
Violation was established at a revocation hearing
enhancements: New criminal offense while on probation
notes: Court may revoke probation and impose the original sentence, modify conditions, or continue probation. Burden of proof is preponderance of the evidence.

offense_class: Depends on underlying offense
elements: Defendant was released on parole
Defendant violated a condition of parole
Violation was established at a revocation hearing
notes: Board of Parole makes revocation decisions. May revoke parole and return to prison for remaining time. Less Restrictive Parole Revocation Act (LIRRA) may limit reincarceration for technical violations.

statute_title: Criminal Liability for Conduct of Another
offense_class: Same as principal offense
elements: Defendant, acting with the mental culpability required for the offense
Solicited, requested, commanded, importuned, or intentionally aided another
To engage in the prohibited conduct
notes: An accomplice is criminally liable to the same extent as the principal. Affirmative defense if defendant's conduct was not reasonably foreseeable.

offense_class: One class lower than the completed offense (Class A-I attempted = Class B; Class B attempted = Class C; etc.)
penalty_max: Varies by class of attempted offense (one grade lower)
fine_max: Varies by class of attempted offense
elements: Defendant, with intent to commit a crime
Engaged in conduct which tended to effect the commission of such crime
notes: Attempt reduces the offense by one grade. Attempted Class A-I Felony becomes Class B Felony. Attempted Class B Felony becomes Class C Felony, and so on.

offense_class: Class E Felony (4th — conspiracy to commit any felony); Higher degrees for more serious targets
elements: Defendant, with intent that conduct constituting a felony be performed
Agreed with one or more persons to engage in or cause the performance of such conduct
One or more conspirators committed an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy
enhancements: Conspiracy to commit Class B or C Felony (3rd degree — Class D under § 105.13)
Conspiracy to commit Class A Felony (2nd degree — Class C under § 105.15)
Conspiracy to commit Class A-I Felony (1st degree — Class B under § 105.17)
notes: Six degrees of conspiracy in New York. Graded based on the seriousness of the target offense. Requires an overt act. Renunciation defense available if defendant voluntarily thwarts the conspiracy.
